quote: In Prism, it's easy to: Drag the wrong data into a chart ... Forget which condition was which ... Copy-paste the wrong result into your figure
problem: Manual drag-and-drop/copy-paste between data, results and figures produces silent errors and loses track of conditions
need: Keep data, statistics and figure linked so a figure is always regenerated from the source table, with an audit trail of every change

quote: So if you're still manually replotting qPCR data for the third time this week, maybe it's time to ask: "Is it me... or is it the tool?"
problem: Repeated experiments force manual re-plotting of the same qPCR figure each time new data arrive
need: Template a finished analysis+graph so new runs of the same assay can be dropped in and replotted automatically (batch)

quote: Prism lives in a world of drag-and-drop, local files, and single-user workflows.
problem: Point-and-click tool files are local and single-user, poorly suited to team projects and version control
need: Shareable projects that a whole team can open, review and version without per-seat desktop installs

quote: Often, folks from my lab will take an R course and spend a half-day making some plots of the iris dataset or calculating miles per gallon using mtcars . Once they leave the room, it is hard for them to connect what they learned to a real-life use case in the lab.
problem: Generic programming courses do not transfer to the lab members' own experiments
need: Teach and guide with the user's own assay data (e.g. Fiji per-image outputs) rather than toy datasets

workflow: microscopy: one Fiji output text file per image -> figure
quote: The output of the analysis is plain text files, one for each image. To make a figure, we need to process all of these text files and turn them into publication-quality figures
problem: Image analysis yields dozens of per-image files that must be merged with condition/replicate labels before plotting
need: Import a folder of per-image result files at once, deriving condition and experimental repeat from file or folder names

workflow: microscopy file naming through to analysis
quote: For example, when they are at the microscope, naming files is important because they get carried through: to the Fiji step and then into R. Any inconsistencies cause headaches.
problem: Inconsistent file names at acquisition break the downstream merge of conditions/replicates
need: Tolerant import that previews parsed condition/replicate labels from file names and flags inconsistencies before analysis

workflow: excluding a bad experimental repeat and replotting
quote: Next, explain that the person who did the experiments found out that the rapamycin used in the 4th experiment, was prepared from a stock solution which was at the wrong concentration. How can we exclude the n4 data and remake a new SuperPlot
problem: Need to exclude one whole biological repeat and regenerate the replicate-aware plot and stats
need: Allow excluding an entire experimental repeat (with a recorded reason) and auto-refresh SuperPlot and test on replicate means

quote: Very intuitive and plots are super easy to customise (changing plot design with ggplot2 always requires lots of googling for me). R defs has the edge of being a free software, whereas Prism is not.
problem: Free code-based plotting is hard to customise without constant searching; the easy GUI tool costs money
need: GUI-level ease of customising violin/box plots without licence cost

quote: I know the price is an issue but if the school can grant access somehow, graphpad prism allows for data vizualisation and some basic data analysis. Not as much freedom in it as youd have with R though.
problem: Access to the preferred tool depends on the institution paying; the tool also restricts freedom compared to code
need: Freely accessible tool with enough flexibility not to force a move to code

role: PI/editor (Mary Williams, Plantae) summarising reader questions
workflow: replacing bar graphs with violin graphs
quote: I mentioned the greater usefulness of violin graphs over bar graphs. Naturally, several people asked for suggestions about how to make a violin graph.
problem: Researchers told to move beyond bar graphs do not know which tool can make a violin plot
need: Offer violin/box/dot plots as first-class graph types, one click from a bar graph

quote: I have to say violin plots are not better than boxplot for small sample sizes (n < 30). Violin plots show the distribution shape, but it's impossible to know the exact distribution w/o a large n. For n < 100 I'd recommend boxplot w/ all dots jittered.
problem: Violin plots mislead at the small n typical of bench experiments
need: Recommend the plot type from n (e.g. warn on violin with n<30; default to box + all points)

quote: The tidy data structure is different from the popular spreadsheet format and (in my experience) not intuitive to grasp. Therefore, the conversion of ordinary, spreadsheet data into this structure may present a considerable bottleneck for creating superplots.
problem: Wide spreadsheet layouts must be converted to tidy/long format before replicate-aware plots can be made
need: Accept wide spreadsheets (condition and replicate as header rows) and convert to long format automatically

quote: The reason is that duplicate column names (as present in this file) are not accepted and will be modified.
problem: Typical lab sheets with repeated condition headers break standard importers
need: Import multi-row headers with duplicate names (condition x replicate) without mangling them

workflow: statistics in experiment planning and analysis
quote: Bioscience students are especially guilty of this. Taking statistics courses early on is useful. However, don't be discouraged if it all goes over your head at first.
problem: Bioscience students avoid statistics and find courses go over their heads
need: In-context guidance on replicates and test choice at the moment of analysis

quote: I have attended one particular course two times before it really became useful, because I had my own data to practice with by the second time.
problem: Statistics training only sticks when applied to one's own data
need: Explanations attached to the user's own dataset and results, not abstract

workflow: omics data analysis by wet-lab labs
quote: But the analysis of these data can take months. Labs can't afford to pay anyone to do that. Also, the wet-lab scientist knows best what to look for in their data. But without the skills to do the data analysis themselves, these labs get stuck.
problem: Wet labs generate omics data but lack skills or funds to analyse it
need: Self-serve PCA / MA / volcano analyses for wet-lab scientists without coding

quote: I have no talent for programming but this training was exactly what I hoped it would be. The basics are not as scary as I thought. I can now judge the quality of analyses in my own work and others and avoid pitfalls.
problem: PI felt unable to judge analysis quality without programming skills
need: Transparent analyses whose steps a non-programmer can inspect and judge

workflow: peer review of quantitative cell biology
quote: One concern of mine is that real knowledge in quantitative methods is scarce and yet as it permeates mainstream biology, there is a lack of prepared peer reviewers.
problem: Quantitative analyses are spreading in cell biology faster than reviewers can check them
need: Analysis reports that state the test, n and assumptions explicitly so reviewers can verify them

quote: I know Universities where cutting Mathematics/Statistics modules from our Biology courses has been considered. The reason: "the students find it tough"
problem: Biology students arrive with weak statistics training because courses are cut
need: Assume minimal statistics background: built-in plain-language explanations for each test

quote: The people with no prior experience found the final session pretty tough so I don't think it would be possible to go through this material in fewer sessions.
problem: Going from zero to a real figure in R needs multiple taught sessions even with a PI teaching
need: Path from raw lab data to finished figure that does not need multi-session programming training

quote: Of course, the best way to learn is by doing, so the challenge is to get people to persist with R for their number crunching. A simple way is to keep advocating for analysis to be done in R or more drastically, other software could be outlawed.
problem: Lab members drift back to other software after R training
need: Lower ongoing friction so reproducible analysis does not need policing

workflow: time-course plots of single-cell ratio imaging
quote: Some time ago, my favorite (commercial) software package for making graphs was no longer supported due to a system upgrade. So I was looking for a powerful and flexible alternative for data visualization.
problem: A commercial graphing package stopped working after an OS upgrade, stranding the user's workflow
need: Platform-independent tool (e.g. browser-based) whose files keep opening after OS upgrades

workflow: time-course: mean + 95% CI ribbon over single-cell traces
quote: The instruction to plot graphs with ggplot() usually consists of several different functions and may be daunting at first sight.
problem: Layered code graphs (individual traces + mean + CI band + stimulus box) are daunting for wet-lab users
need: Time-course graph with individual traces in grey, mean with 95% CI ribbon and shaded stimulus intervals as built-in options

quote: I have also, over the years, encountered problems where students have stored data in spreadsheets and then had the program change all there gene names/tracking codes etc. to a 'correct' value. This has resulted in months of work lost and confused.
problem: Spreadsheet autocorrect silently converts gene names/IDs, losing months of work
need: Never auto-convert identifiers on paste/import; keep text columns as text and flag date-like coercions

quote: There is no indication whether the date is mm/dd/yyyy or dd/mm/yyyy, hence the program may change 01/10/2011 to either the 1st October 2011, or the 10th January 2011.
problem: Ambiguous date formats and stripped leading zeros corrupt data on entry
need: Locale-explicit date parsing and preservation of leading zeros on import

role: Nature news (reporting analysis by bioinformatician Mark Ziemann)
quote: Despite geneticists being warned about spreadsheet problems, 30% of published papers contain mangled gene names in supplementary data.
problem: Spreadsheet autocorrect corrupts gene names in a large share of published papers
need: Data entry that treats identifiers as text and warns about auto-converted values before export

role: statistician (Karl Broman, quoted in Nature Technology feature)
workflow: working on raw data in spreadsheets
quote: Every time you interact with Excel is an opportunity to accidentally type something extra somewhere and not realize it
problem: Raw data in spreadsheets is silently altered by stray keystrokes
need: Keep raw data read-only/locked and do analysis on derived copies with change history

role: data scientist (Heidi Seibold, quoted in Nature Technology feature)
quote: an analysis that happens inside a spreadsheet using pointing and clicking is hard to follow and even harder to replicate.
problem: Point-and-click analyses leave no replayable record
need: Record every GUI step as a replayable, exportable analysis log/script

role: research software technician (Obose Eselebor, quoted in Nature Technology feature)
quote: She recalls a time when what should have been a quick peek at a spreadsheet with 100,000 rows kept freezing her laptop.
problem: Spreadsheet software freezes on 100,000-row data sets
need: Handle 100k+ row tables smoothly (virtualised grid, streaming import)

role: bioinformatics director (Ming Tommy Tang, quoted in Nature Technology feature)
quote: Collaborations between bioinformaticians and wet-laboratory researchers can become frustrating if both sides don't clearly communicate what they're doing and what they need.
problem: Hand-offs between wet-lab and bioinformatics people are frustrating
need: Shareable analysis files that show data, steps and assumptions to both bench and computational collaborators

role: institutional analysis hub (King's College London HAB) news post
quote: Following the recent announcement that GraphPad Prism will now require subscriptions, the HAB will be offering a new series of hands-on workshops for non-coders.
problem: Licensing change forces a whole faculty to consider retraining non-coders to redo their Prism analyses in R
need: Free tool that covers the everyday Prism analyses (t-tests, ANOVA, regression, mixed models, graphs) without retraining in code

role: cell biologist / microscopist (Sam Lord, blog author)
quote: But a concerning outcome of this trend is that, when authors decide to plot every measurement or every cell as a separate datapoint, it seems to trick people into thinking that each cell is an independent sample.
problem: Plotting every cell encourages treating cells as independent n, inflating significance
need: When per-cell data carry a replicate label, test on replicate means by default and warn if n = number of cells

role: cell biologist / microscopist (Sam Lord, blog author)
quote: I scanned the latest issues of popular cell biology journals and found that over half the papers counted each cell as a separate
problem: More than half of sampled cell biology papers pseudo-replicate (each cell = n)
need: Make the n definition explicit in the analysis and in exported methods text

role: cell biologist / microscopist (Sam Lord, blog author)
quote: On the simplest level, you can simply paste two (or more!) plots in Illustrator and overlay them. Play around with colors and transparency to make it visually appealing, and you're done!
problem: SuperPlots have to be built by overlaying separate plots by hand in Illustrator
need: One-click SuperPlot: cell-level points coloured by replicate with replicate means overlaid and the test run on those means

quote: However, despite all these efforts, dynamite plots continue to be ubiquitous in the scientific literature.
problem: Mean+error bar 'dynamite' plots persist despite years of criticism
need: Default to dot/box plots showing every point for continuous small-n data; make bars an explicit choice

quote: I analyzed these data and inaccurately pasted the data into the analysis software, leading to an incorrect grouping of the data.
problem: Mis-pasted data produced wrong group assignments and a retracted paper
need: Show group membership and n per group clearly after paste/import and keep a link to the raw data file

workflow: replicate readings treated as independent experiments
quote: Actually data show replicate reading of same sample from same experiment. This false statistic analysis make very small error bar so statistic significance is reached.
problem: Technical replicate readings were analysed as independent experiments
need: Ask whether replicates are technical or biological and aggregate technical ones before testing

role: journal ethics committee chair (quoted in Retraction Watch)
quote: We do need to see the individual data points on which these figures and statistics were based.
problem: Journals need individual data points behind summary figures and tests
need: Export figures with underlying point data and analysis record for journal/reviewer requests

workflow: SE vs SD in reported results
quote: Mistaking a standard error for a standard deviation is common and seems to often result from a combination of insufficient carefulness on the part of the meta-analysts and unclear or incorrect labeling of standard errors vs standard deviations in the original articles being meta-analyzed.
problem: Unclear SE/SD labelling in papers leads to downstream errors and retractions
need: Always label error bars and table values explicitly (SD, SEM, 95% CI) in graphs, legends and exports

role: image analysts (Owen Puls & Rachel Lee, blog authors)
quote: And yet, it can be difficult to know where to get started with image analysis, given the abundance of tools and techniques that are available.
problem: Overwhelming tool choice for turning microscopy into numbers that reviewers expect
need: Clear entry path from image-analysis outputs (Fiji/CellProfiler tables) into analysis and graphs

role: life science library staff (Academia Sinica, blog author)
quote: The EC50 (or IC50) should be within range of your data, near the middle of the curve. If these values are not appropriate, it might be useful to constrain some of the parameters. Additionally, check that plateaus of your data are reasonable.
problem: Users must manually judge whether fitted IC50/plateaus are plausible and decide on constraints
need: Automatic fit diagnostics: flag IC50 outside the tested range and plateaus far beyond the data, and suggest constraints

role: life science library staff (Academia Sinica, blog author)
quote: It has so many options that sometimes it can be daunting to learn the hangs of it, but the more you invest in understanding it, the more you will get out of it, and when stuck, you can always reach out to someone for help!
problem: The number of options in the analysis package is daunting for new users
need: Progressive disclosure: sensible defaults first, advanced options only when needed

role: lab wiki, neuroscience EM lab (Harris lab, UT Austin)
quote: Information on this page is based on a Windows PC with Adobe Photoshop version 23.0 (and later), Adobe Illustrator version 26.0 (and later), and GraphPad Prism 9. Also requires basic knowledge of Microsoft Excel, Microsoft PowerPoint, Reconstruct, and maybe Fiji/ImageJ.
problem: Producing one publication figure requires a chain of five or more separate (mostly paid) programs
need: Produce journal-ready multi-panel figures (sizes, fonts, vector export) without a multi-program chain

role: lab wiki, neuroscience EM lab (Harris lab, UT Austin)
quote: Output from GraphPad Prism: export as EPS, then open in Illustrator
problem: Graphs must be exported and reopened in Illustrator to assemble figures
need: Clean vector (EPS/PDF/SVG) export with editable text and true sizing so graphs drop into figure layouts unchanged

role: lab wiki, neuroscience EM lab (Harris lab, UT Austin)
quote: Every journal has its own figure format, so pay attention to what they are asking for. Not following the instructions can result in published figures with a sub-optimal resolution, shifted colors, shifted brightness/contrast, etc., etc.
problem: Journal-specific size/resolution/colour rules are easy to get wrong
need: Journal presets for figure width, minimum font size, colour mode and DPI at export

role: lab wiki, neuroscience EM lab (Harris lab, UT Austin)
quote: Remember that your software tools may have their own default font (e.g., Calibri for Microsoft Office and Myriad Pro for Adobe Illustrator). Use the same font across all figures because having different fonts can be distracting.
problem: Different tools' default fonts produce inconsistent figures
need: Project-wide style (font, sizes, condition colours) applied to all graphs

role: flow cytometry trainer, PhD biology (Tim Bushnell, stated)
quote: Before you move to hypothesis testing, it is often best to convert this data to a fold over background, or resolution metric (R
problem: MFI data need conversion (fold over background / resolution metric using median and robust SD) before testing
need: Flow-cytometry-aware analysis: median/rSD summaries, fold-over-background or resolution metric, then one-sample test vs 0

quote: However, generating these plots remains relatively difficult. Commercial plotting software are widely available but are often expensive and constitute a financial burden for academic labs and students alike. Free alternatives exist but mostly require coding knowledge (i.e., R language).
problem: Better-than-bar plots are either expensive (commercial) or require coding
need: Free, no-code tool for dot/box/violin plots with paste-in data and editable PDF export

quote: the resulting graphs can be exported as images or modifiable PDFs. PlotsOfData was written using the powerful R/shiny and implements the well-known ggplot2 package for generating plots. I have already used this tool to generate plots for my current manuscript
problem: Researcher needs plots that remain editable after export for figure assembly
need: Export editable vector PDF/SVG plus raster images

role: data scientist, fly neuroscience lab (Joses Ho, interviewed author)
workflow: getting other labs to use estimation statistics
quote: I also attempted to get other laboratories to use my Python code, but the need to learn programming was a major barrier to adoption, so it became clear I needed to be able to say: "There's an app for that."
problem: Better statistics methods do not spread to bench labs when they require programming
need: Provide estimation plots (effect size + CI with raw data) in a no-code tool

role: data scientist, fly neuroscience lab (Joses Ho, interviewed author)
quote: So it really grew out of our own frustration with significance testing, and a desire for better tools for ourselves.
problem: Lab frustrated by P-value-only significance testing
need: Report effect size with bootstrap CI alongside or instead of P values

role: PI, molecular and cell biology (Adam Claridge-Chang, quoted)
workflow: two-group comparisons presented as bar charts with P values
quote: For experimental outcomes, this false dichotomy constrains interpretation to the presence or absence of an effect, instead of a more meaningful consideration of effect size
problem: P-value significant/non-significant framing hides effect magnitude
need: Default output shows effect size and its CI with the raw data, not just a significance verdict

quote: it condemned the rather common and erroneous practice of depicting means and SD/SEM on bar graphs in figures, and analyzing that data with a non-parametric test which does not look at means, such as the Mann Whitney U test. Sadly, this practice still exists, even in journals as hallowed as Nature.
problem: Graph summary (mean +/- SEM bars) and test (rank-based Mann-Whitney) disagree
need: Keep the plotted summary consistent with the test (medians/IQR with rank tests; means/CI with t-tests) and warn on mismatch

quote: I think the problems come when the statistician isn't seen as a collaborator, but as a workman or a servant. The Beast thinks of me as a servant too, but he never annoys me with questions about why he can't just do a t-test.
problem: Biologists push statisticians to just run a t-test regardless of design
need: Explain in plain language why a design needs something other than a t-test

quote: Programming tools can speed up and strengthen analyses, but mastering the skills takes time and can be daunting.
problem: Programming skills that would strengthen analyses are daunting and slow to acquire
need: Strong analyses available without programming mastery

quote: Sadly, 65% of papers published in 2015 reported the SEM to (presumably) summarize data variability, while another 12.5% of papers included figures with error bars that were not defined (!).
problem: SEM used to describe variability and error bars left undefined in most papers
need: Prompt for the purpose of the error bar (describe spread -> SD; precision -> 95% CI) and always print its definition in the legend

quote: When authors report p<0.05, it is unclear whether the p-value is p=0.013 or p=0.049 or p=0.00001. In my audit of published papers, only 58% consistently reported exact p-values.
problem: Inexact P values (p<0.05) hide the actual result
need: Report exact P values by default in results tables, graph annotations and methods text

quote: Of the papers audited that reported p-values between 0.05-0.1, 57% of them interpreted these p-values as statistically significant or statistical trends.
problem: Near-threshold P values are spun as significant 'trends'
need: Results wording that states effect size and CI and does not label p>alpha as significant or a trend

workflow: SEM in figures by journal convention
quote: In their response to my comments, the authors explained they changed the SEM to SD in text, but kept the SEM in figures because this was the convention for the Journal of Neurophysiology!
problem: Authors keep SEM error bars in figures because of field convention, contradicting text
need: Keep error-bar type consistent between figure and text and explain the choice

workflow: time-course plots of mean +/- error bars
quote: However, when a plot reveals a pattern over time, humans may erroneously conclude, consciously or not, that each subject or sample used to compute these summary statistics follow the same overall pattern.
problem: Mean time-course plots hide divergent individual trajectories
need: Option to overlay individual subject traces under the mean time course

quote: In my experience, presenting the standard deviation when the standard error in the mean is appropriate is the much more common error.
problem: Readers disagree on which error bar is appropriate; the SD/SEM choice remains confusing
need: Explain SD vs SEM vs CI at the point of choice, based on whether the goal is to describe spread or estimate the mean

workflow: small-n lab studies shown as bar graphs
quote: That is, presenting SE error bars magnifies an apparent visual difference between groups
problem: SE bars on bar graphs exaggerate apparent group differences in small samples
need: Default to scatter (all points) for small n, with SD or CI overlay

role: lab blog, cell biology (Sardana lab, Cornell)
quote: The problem of comically miniscule (and hence useless) P-values in many cell biology studies is in part due to erroneous and inflated sample size, N. N should represent the number of times an experiment is repeated, not the total number of cells.
problem: N inflated by counting cells yields meaninglessly small P values
need: Make the experimental unit explicit and compute tests on per-replicate summaries

role: lab blog, cell biology (Sardana lab, Cornell)
workflow: cell migration speed, 3 replicates x 200 cells
quote: first calculate the mean of those 200 measurements for each sample, then run a t-test on those sample means (three control, three treated).
problem: Researchers must aggregate cell measurements to replicate means by hand before testing
need: Automatic per-replicate aggregation and colour-coded beeswarm SuperPlot from long-format cell data

role: assistant professor, molecular cytology (Joachim Goedhart; colour vision deficiency, stated)
quote: One of the recommendations is to use a color blindness simulator. Having a color vision deficiency myself,
problem: Default category colours are not readable by colour-blind researchers/readers
need: Colour-blind-safe default palettes and a built-in colour-vision-deficiency preview

quote: Additionally, many scientists are not able to afford commercial licenses for more mainstream programs that take care of data analysis and visualization, which can sometimes lead to inadequate data assessing and analysis.
problem: Unaffordable commercial licences push scientists toward inadequate analysis
need: Free tool with the standard analyses and graph types so cost does not degrade analysis quality

quote: Unfortunately, existing open-source tools often have complex syntax, posing a barrier for life scientists especially those not used to work with code. Traditional data analysis workflows can't really cope with the increasing data volume and current reproducibility standards.
problem: Free tools have complex syntax; manual workflows fail on volume and reproducibility
need: Low-syntax interface that still records reproducible, rerunnable analysis steps

role: university medical library software licensing page
quote: Personal Prism licenses cost $150 per person per license year.
problem: Recurring per-person annual cost charged to labs (vs $40 per computer announced by the same library in 2017)
need: No per-seat recurring licence for core lab statistics and graphing

quote: Becker Library is pleased to announce the annual license fee for GraphPad Prism has been reduced to $40 per computer.
problem: Licence cost depends on institutional volume deals; earlier per-computer fee later replaced by much higher per-person fee
need: Predictable, low or zero cost access independent of institutional purchasing

role: MPhil candidate, plant epigenetics; former wet-lab student (stated)
workflow: learning coding for data analysis from a wet-lab background
quote: Coming from a non-coding background, for me the letters and symbols of different coding functions seemed like ancient hieroglyphs that I couldn't comprehend.
problem: Code syntax is incomprehensible to wet-lab-trained students
need: Analysis without writing code, with optional code export for those who want it

role: MPhil candidate, plant epigenetics; former wet-lab student (stated)
quote: At first, I found it overwhelming to understand what happens once a code is executed. This was because I knew too little at the time to check the processed data files and interpret the output.
problem: Cannot verify what an analysis step did or interpret its output
need: Show intermediate results and plain-language interpretation of each output

role: MPhil candidate, plant epigenetics; former wet-lab student (stated)
quote: I also faced problems understanding the terminologies used in computational biology - hierarchical clustering, principal component analysis (PCA), and bootstrapping, just to name a few of these terms.
problem: Jargon of multivariate methods blocks understanding
need: Inline glossary/explanations for PCA, clustering and bootstrap outputs

quote: There was still a big gap in knowledge and communication between pure biologists and bioinformaticians here at Cambridge, despite it being one of the most resourceful pioneers in research transformation.
problem: Knowledge/communication gap between bench biologists and bioinformaticians
need: Tools wet-lab scientists can use themselves for routine analyses, with outputs bioinformaticians can audit

role: lab website, molecular biology (Onish lab, Colorado State)
quote: The interpretation of data we generate as biologists is often incomplete without the proper implementation of statistical tools. However, it is commonplace for biologists to be deficient in statistical thinking.
problem: Labs need to run their own statistics workshops because biologists lack statistical thinking
need: Built-in statistics guidance that teaches while analysing

workflow: cell area under three conditions, skewed data
quote: Therefore, p-values fail to answer a very relevant question: "How large is the difference between the conditions?"
problem: P values do not tell bench scientists how large the effect is
need: Report difference of medians/means vs control with bootstrap 95% CI and plot it beside the data

quote: When the distribution of the observed areas is non-normal (as is the case here), the median better reflects the central tendency (i.e. typical value) of the sample.
problem: Skewed per-cell measurements need median-based summaries and effect sizes
need: Detect skew and offer median differences with bootstrap CIs

quote: However, in life science we often have bimodal distributions, clusters, or gaps. Then boxplots become very insufficient and might even conceal interesting aspects (if not outright be misleading).
problem: Box plots hide bimodality and gaps common in life-science data
need: Offer histogram/density/violin + points, and flag apparent multimodality

quote: Here, one has to be very careful with choosing bin sizes: too large or too small bins can greatly distort the histogram shape and result in a misleading chart.
problem: Histogram bin choice can distort the distribution
need: Sensible automatic binning with an interactive bin-width control

quote: One thing to keep in mind I think is to avoid over-interpretation of the raw data. When you say "that zebras show a curious clustering" it shows more a weakness of raw points to me because our brain tends to seek for patterns of all kinds
problem: Showing all points invites over-interpretation of chance patterns
need: Pair raw points with summaries and uncertainty so patterns are judged against noise

role: Executive Director, Future of Research (Gary McDowell, former bench scientist)
quote: There is, however, open admission in the Nature article that current PIs often have not been trained in these methods themselves, so training cannot be expected to come from them.
problem: Trainees cannot learn rigorous analysis from PIs who were never trained in it
need: Analysis tool that embeds rigor checks (replicates, blinding, design) so good practice does not depend on the PI

role: Executive Director, Future of Research (Gary McDowell)
quote: How is the biomedical research enterprise ensuring that rigorous scientific research is taking place, if training in rigor and reproducibility is expected to be carried out in a non-standard, individual manner by the trainees themselves, despite a lack of protected time for any training?
problem: No protected time for trainees to learn statistics/rigor
need: Just-in-time guidance inside the analysis rather than separate courses

workflow: first data analysis as a new biologist
quote: If you're a baby biologist, you may soon encounter one of your first hurdles: data analysis. Excel, Prism, R, there are lots of options for analyzing your data, and they all have different purposes.
problem: New biologists face data analysis as an early hurdle with confusing tool choice
need: One accessible starting point covering everyday lab analyses and graphs

workflow: access to analysis software for students
quote: other software that you may use to analyze data, like Prism, for example, may not be accessible to someone just starting out, since it comes with a cost of about $150/year.
problem: Annual licence cost makes standard lab software inaccessible to beginners
need: Free access for students and early-career researchers

role: retraction notice quoted in Retraction Watch
quote: In Figure 5, there was an error in statistical analysis of quantitative Western blot data, resulting in error bars that were too small.
problem: Wrong statistical handling of densitometry data produced too-small error bars and a retraction
need: Densitometry-to-statistics workflow that aggregates lanes/blots correctly and states n and error type

quote: In one case I alerted the authors to this problem, and their response was simply to dial back all the blots in powerpoint (using brightness/contrast), resulting in gray fat bands instead of black fat bands.
problem: Saturated bands are quantified anyway; contrast tweaks hide saturation
need: Detect saturated (flat-topped) lane profiles from raw images and refuse/flag quantification

quote: The dynamic range of most traditional western blot methods (i.e., ECL plus film) is about 10 fold. In reality it is more like 5-7 fold. It is simply impossible to measure a greater than a 5-7 fold change in the level of a protein using such methods.
problem: Reported fold changes exceed the linear range of the detection method
need: Warn when reported densitometry fold changes exceed the validated linear range of the method

quote: All his Western blot bands were saturated and when the post-doc was challenged it was quite clear he had no idea about basic densitometry.
problem: Trainees quantify saturated blots without understanding densitometry basics
need: Built-in densitometry checks and explanations (saturation, background, linear range)

role: statistician supporting animal researchers (Simon Bate, GSK; questions from researchers)
workflow: choosing n for animal / cell experiments
quote: I often hear "we always use n=6" or "the other researchers use n=6, so shall we". Needless to say, this is not a recommended approach.
problem: Sample sizes are copied by habit instead of calculated from the lab's own variability
need: Power/sample-size calculator fed by variability from the user's previous data, with power curves over a range of effect sizes

role: statistician supporting animal researchers (question asked by researchers)
quote: My results are interesting but not statistically significant. Can I test more animals/batches of cells until I reach p<0.05?
problem: Researchers want to keep adding batches until p<0.05 (optional stopping)
need: Pre-registered n with warnings against sequential top-ups, or proper group-sequential designs with adjusted alpha

role: statistician supporting animal researchers (Simon Bate, GSK)
workflow: repeating a small experiment three times
